synopsis: Automatic braking requires a new, machine-specific hazard analysis: missed braking and unsafe or unnecessary intervention must be assessed separately, and neither stopping sooner nor matching the old warning system establishes safety [f1977, f118, f11891, f10529]. Its scope must include pedestrian strikes, shifted loads, downhill and loss-of-control cases, and post-brake hazards such as rollaway, brake latching and second collisions during restart; downhill and loss-of-control cases were omitted from the booklet's eight questions [f3102, f3400, f6599, f3630]. ISO 19014-1 requires safety analysis to determine risk reduction and machine performance level, while Part 5 tables can avoid a full analysis for every new model; ISO 13849-1:2023 alone does not specify the collision function's required performance level [f10516, f2076, f2350]. Validation should trace requirements, scenarios, tests and acceptance criteria to named hazards and justify coverage of the operating population; statistical methods cannot repair missing hazard classes or an unvalidated simulator [f11969, f8030, f9730, f650]. The indicative plan starts hazard-analysis and scenario work on 1 October 2026 for 90 days, calls for a machine-readable hierarchy during October 2026 to mid-2027, and requires approved intervention analysis before prototype arrival to avoid consuming the four-month validation window in debate [f893, f7361, f11970]. Risk prioritization should not be driven by a 5-by-5 heat map, because the corpus reports ranking defects and range compression in such matrices [f9894, f9442, f9895].

relations.note: Both require separate analysis of missed braking and unsafe or unnecessary braking.
The regulatory chapter frames the two failure categories as separate safety functions.
Both require intervention-specific analysis and separate ratings for false activation and missed detection.
Both reject assuming an earlier emergency stop is safe without analyzing secondary hazards.
The new intervention analysis must determine assurance targets, not comparison with the warning system.
Adds brake latching, acknowledgment, reset and second-collision prevention to post-stop analysis.
The glossary restates brake locking, release rollaway and restart collision hazards.
NIOSH's warning about technology-created hazards supports assessing automatic braking's secondary hazards.
Adds approval timing, intervention requirements, performance-level allocation and test traceability.
Places Part 5 tables within the lifecycle alongside Part 1 risk-based allocation.
Adds a coverage rationale to hazard-to-scenario traceability.
Specifies scenario standards and ranked physical effects for an assessor-quality coverage argument.
Scenario counts without risk taxonomy explain why traceability and coverage rationale are needed.
Both report ranking defects in risk heat maps.
Mis-ranking and range compression justify excluding heat maps from prioritization decisions.
Explains why pre-prototype approval protects the four-month evidence-gathering window.
Gives the planning work an explicit 1 October 2026 start and 90-day duration.
The worked loader-pedestrian critical-risk scenario reinforces prioritizing pedestrian strikes.
